title: Network Protocols for System Design
summary: HTTP, TCP, UDP, and RPC: what each one promises, what it costs, and how to fail safely.
keyPoints: HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol; method semantics decide what is safe to retry.
TCP gives an ordered, reliable byte stream at the cost of handshakes and head-of-line blocking.
UDP gives low overhead and no delivery guarantee; use it when late data is worse than lost data.
RPC fits controlled internal calls; REST fits stable resource-oriented public APIs.
Every network call needs a deadline, and every retry needs a limit and an idempotency plan.

complexity.note: Useful as a lower bound, not a production estimate.
Does not remove TCP head-of-line blocking.

commonMistakes: Retrying a POST without an idempotency key and creating duplicate work.
Setting a timeout only on the client while internal calls wait forever.
Using UDP for data that must arrive completely and in order without building that layer.
Assuming HTTP/2 removes every head-of-line blocking problem.
Using a chatty RPC design that turns one page load into dozens of sequential round trips.
interviewNotes: State the protocol at each boundary and why it fits.
Give deadlines in milliseconds, not the word 'fast'.
Say which operations are idempotent and how writes are protected.
Mention connection pooling and keep-alive when connection setup is a meaningful cost.

checkYourself.question: Why is PUT idempotent but POST usually not?
checkYourself.answer: A PUT replaces a resource at a known address, so repeating it produces the same state. A POST usually creates a new resource or triggers work, so repeating it can create a duplicate.

checkYourself.question: When would you choose UDP over TCP?
checkYourself.answer: When low latency matters more than guaranteed delivery, such as real-time voice, video, or games, and when the application can tolerate or repair loss.

checkYourself.question: What does a deadline protect?
checkYourself.answer: It bounds how long a caller waits, freeing connections and threads. Without one, a slow dependency can exhaust the caller's capacity.
